title: The Posture Review: Sarajevo Weighs Offensive Against Endurance
sources: ICTY Hadžihasanović & Kubura Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T), ARBiH command findings
content:
A war fought without a clear path to victory still demands periodic decisions about how to fight it. For the Sarajevo government, whose army the ICTY Hadžihasanović & Kubura Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T) describes as a force assembling its command structures under fire, the recurring question was one of posture: whether to press offensives that might recover ground but bleed scarce manpower, or to consolidate and endure in the expectation that time, attrition, and shifting international opinion favoured a state defending its recognized borders.

Each option carried a distinct logic and a distinct cost. To press the offensive was to assert that the war could be moved toward a better outcome by force — a posture that suited a government refusing to accept territorial losses as permanent, but one that spent lives and ammunition the arms embargo made nearly irreplaceable. To consolidate and defend was to husband strength behind the lines the safe-area regime of UN Security Council Resolution 836 (1993) nominally protected, accepting a static map in exchange for survival. To signal openness to negotiation, or to accept ceasefire terms, was to convert military restraint into diplomatic position — buying time and international goodwill at the price of momentum.

For the ARBiH, the calculus was shaped by a structural asymmetry the army could not escape. Against a Bosnian Serb force richly supplied with the artillery and armour of the former Yugoslav army, offensive action was costly out of all proportion to the ground it gained. Endurance, by contrast, played to the one advantage the government held: a cause the international community was increasingly disposed to defend, and a population for whom the war was existential rather than territorial.

The posture review was therefore less a choice of strategy than a choice of which scarce resource to spend — lives now, in pursuit of recovery, or time, in the hope that the war’s terms would improve. Pressing the offensive gambled on force; settling toward negotiation gambled on patience. Both were wagers; neither was free.
